newsitem.title: USA: Dollar tumbles on worries over Japan trade surplus.
newsitem.headline: Dollar tumbles on worries over Japan trade surplus.

text.p: The dollar fell sharply Monday for the second consecutive session as concerns mounted over Japan's growing trade surplus and Europe's plan to launch a single currency.

The dollar fell as low as 1.7020 German marks in early U.S. trading, 4 pfennigs below the 39-month high reached Friday in European trade, and dropped to a six-month low of 111.80 Japanese yen in Asian trade as nerves frayed ahead of Wednesday's scheduled release of fresh Japanese trade figures.
The U.S. currency closed lower Monday at 1.7065 marks from 1.7247 at Friday's U.S. close and 112.90 yen from 114.37.

The dollar's slide was first sparked Friday when U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky reiterated recent comments from U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin that Japan could not rely on exports to lift its economy out of recession.
A weak yen makes Japanese goods relatively less expensive for foreign buyers and dealers worried pressure from Washington could push the yen higher vs. the dollar.

"People are concerned about the Japanese current account numbers on Wednesday. They are expecting a further widening of the trade surplus that Japan has with the U.S. and people are buying yen on that," said Doug Lee, a corporate dealer at Sakura Bank Ltd.

Shaking the dollar from its perch against the mark was news that a meeting of European finance ministers Monday failed to agree on final details of a stability pact aimed at ensuring spending discipline among countries to be joined in monetary union.

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told his European Union (EU) counterparts at a meeting in Luxembourg that the newly formed French government needed more time to study the bloc's stability pact, an intergral part of its plans for economic and monetary union.

Foreign exchange markets have been in turmoil recently over whether Europe will meet the 1999 launch date for a single currency, to be called the euro, and whether the strict fiscal criteria required for membership will be weakened.

"The longer this goes on ... without some sort of resolution or positive talk, the more people are getting a little bit wary of being short marks and they are starting to look at being long marks as an opportunity," said Elliott Dix, an assistant vice president at Signet Bank in Richmond, Va.
Strauss-Kahn said there would be further discussions with France's EU partners in the coming days, notably at a Franco-German summit in Poitiers in western France Friday.
But asked whether he thought the EU could complete talks on the stability pact in time for a summit in Amsterdam on June 16-17, he said: "I don't believe we can complete it between now and then."
The Amsterdam summit had been expected to approve the pact, which was largely agreed to by EU leaders at a Dublin summit last December.

Strauss-Kahn reassured the financial markets that the euro would be launched on time, but the dollar bottomed out against the mark after Bundesbank council member Raimut Jochimsen called for strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria for membership in monetary union.

Jochimsen said the need to maintain strict convergence criteria was greater than the need for a timely start, playing on dollar bulls' fears of a delay to the 1999 lauch date for the euro and strengthening the mark.
The dollar took little comfort in Rubin's oft-stated remark that the United States favours a strong dollar.
In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.4385 Swiss francs from 1.4497 and rose to Canadian $1.3882 from C$1.3837. The pound rose to $1.6373 from $1.6320.
